Name: multihop_latent_intermediate
Title: The Missing Middle: Latent Intermediate Entities in Two-Hop Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: For two-hop factual questions ('the capital of the country where X was born'), models that answer correctly form a decodable representation of the intermediate entity in middle layers at the relevant token position, and answering fails precisely when this latent intermediate is absent or weak. The intermediate representation is the causal bottleneck, not merely a correlate.
Related Work: Yang et al. (2024) and Biran et al. (2024) probe latent multi-hop reasoning and 'back-patching'. Press et al. (2023) show compositionality gaps behaviorally. We sharpen the causal claim: the intermediate entity representation is a necessary bottleneck whose strength predicts and, when patched in, causally rescues correct two-hop answers-distinguishing genuine latent composition from shortcut co-occurrence.
Abstract: Multi-hop factual questions require composing two stored facts through an intermediate entity that is never mentioned in the prompt. We test whether models solve these by materializing the intermediate entity internally and whether that representation is causally necessary. Using two-hop questions with known bridge entities, we train probes to decode the bridge entity from residual states across layers and positions, and we perform causal patching: transplanting the bridge representation from a correct run into a failing run. We hypothesize that (i) the bridge entity is decodable in middle layers before the second hop resolves, (ii) bridge decodability predicts answer correctness, (iii) patching a strong bridge representation into a failing run rescues the correct answer, and (iv) when models answer via shortcut (direct subject-object co-occurrence) the bridge is NOT decodable yet the answer is correct-separating composition from memorized shortcuts. We evaluate across models and relation pairs, and we contrast questions whose two-hop answer also appears as a direct training association against those that do not. Confirming these predictions would establish latent intermediate representations as the causal substrate of compositional recall and provide a probe-based test for whether a given correct answer was reasoned or memorized, with implications for evaluating genuine reasoning.
Experiments: 1. Build two-hop questions with annotated bridge entities; tag each as shortcut-available or not (via corpus co-occurrence). 2. Train probes to decode the bridge across layers/positions. 3. Correlate bridge decodability with correctness. 4. Causal patching: move bridge-carrying states from correct to failing runs; measure answer rescue. 5. Compare shortcut vs non-shortcut items for bridge presence. Metrics: bridge probe accuracy, decodability-correctness correlation, rescue rate, bridge-presence difference between shortcut and non-shortcut.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Identifying the exact token position of the bridge is nontrivial. Shortcut detection via co-occurrence is imperfect. Patching may inject more than the bridge, confounding causality. Some models may compose without a cleanly-localized bridge, weakening the bottleneck claim.
